deployedAtNote: TWO BLOCKS, and the record names which instant it publishes. The oracle went in first, alone, in block 54,989,143 (own timestamp 1788598017 = 2026-09-05T08:46:57Z, read with `cast block`); the six singletons and the three wire calls landed together five seconds later in block 54,989,195 (own timestamp 1788598022 = 2026-09-05T08:47:02Z). `deployedAt` and `deployBlock` are the SECOND block — the instant the protocol became wired and complete. `startBlock` is the FIRST, because an indexer that starts at the second one misses the oracle's own deploy. Both numbers are block timestamps, not the runner's wall clock; the Base Sepolia record carries a note about a one-second wall-clock drift that this record avoids by never reading the clock.
note: The Robinhood Chain mainnet (chain 4663) deployment, ten transactions, every receipt status 1. `sourceCommit` b1cde122 is the tip of origin/protocol/main and is the tree both broadcast scripts were built from. WHAT WAS READ, AND WHY IT WAS READ RATHER THAN COPIED: every address, every wiring edge, every oracle field and every code size below was read from chain 4663 with `cast` at block 54,991,182, pinned with `--block` so the whole table is one consistent state. The broadcast JSON was NOT trusted for any of it, and on this run that was not a precaution but a correction — see `broadcastLabelWarning`. `contracts/config/robinhood-mainnet.json` was likewise not trusted: it is a configuration file, it says of itself that nothing is deployed with it, and it was written the day before this broadcast. broadcastLabelWarning: THE BROADCAST JSON'S `transactions[].hash` COLUMN IS SCRAMBLED ON THIS RUN, and anyone rebuilding this table from `contracts/broadcast/Deploy.s.sol/4663/run-latest.json` will get seven of the nine core rows wrong. Worked example: that file pairs contractName `SubVaultRegistry` with hash 0x653b9df1…, while `cast receipt 0x653b9df1…` returns contractAddress 0xE200d63D… — the OperatorRegistry. The same file's `receipts[]` array is CORRECT (its hash-to-contractAddress-to-gasUsed rows agree with the chain in all ten cases), so the two halves of one file disagree with each other. This is the failure mode `scripts/soak/deployment.mjs`'s header records from Sprint 9, where taking the labels at face value would have swapped VaultFactory and VaultDeployer; it recurred here. The `transactions` table below is built from `cast receipt`, and the contract identities are independently established by `bytecodeCurrency` rather than by any label.

transactions.note: hash, block, gasUsed and txIndex from `cast receipt` for each of the ten hashes; status 1 on all ten. Ordered by execution. `txIndex` is the position within the block and is recorded because the six singletons are not contiguous — other traffic sat between them.

bytecodeCurrency.claim: All seven deployed contracts, and the VaultCore creation code the VaultDeployer carries, are byte-for-byte what sourceCommit b1cde122 builds. Nothing here rests on a code SIZE comparison.
bytecodeCurrency.basis: Two independent byte-level checks, both run 2026-09-05 against the artifacts in the b1cde122 build tree (`contracts/out`, built in a worktree whose only untracked file is a deploy helper). (1) RUNTIME: `cast code <addr> --block 54991182` compared byte-for-byte with each artifact's `deployedBytecode.object`. Every differing byte falls inside a window the artifact itself declares in `deployedBytecode.immutableReferences` — that is, inside a constructor-set immutable, which an artifact necessarily leaves as zeros. Bytes differing OUTSIDE those windows: 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0. (2) CREATION: `cast tx <hash> input` for each of the seven deploys begins with that artifact's `bytecode.object` as an exact prefix, with only ABI-encoded constructor arguments following. The two checks are independent — one reads what is on the chain now, the other reads what was submitted — and they agree.
bytecodeCurrency.whyThisAndNotCodesize: A codesize table would have given a FALSE ALL-CLEAR on precisely the question asked here, because the CBOR metadata trailer is fixed-length and a differently-compiled contract can report an identical size. The Base Sepolia record makes that point and then relies on source-blob identity instead; this record does not need to, because the bytes were compared. The codesize table below is retained only as a cross-check that a wrong CONTRACT was not deployed under a right name — a different and also useful failure.
bytecodeCurrency.whatItDefeats: The scrambled `transactions[].hash` column described in `broadcastLabelWarning` cannot mislabel this table. VaultFactory (3,572 B) and VaultDeployer (938 B) are the pair Sprint 9 actually swapped, and their runtimes are neither the same length nor the same bytes, so a byte-for-byte match against the named artifact identifies each of them independently of every label in the broadcast file.
bytecodeCurrency.reproduce: git checkout b1cde122 && cd contracts && forge build, then compare `out/<Contract>.sol/<Contract>.json` `deployedBytecode.object` with `cast code` as above, masking the artifact's own `immutableReferences` windows. Per scripts/verify-deployment-reproducibility.mjs, only the pinned sourceCommit is guaranteed to reproduce a deployment trailer-for-trailer; HEAD is not.

runtimeCodesize.how: `cast codesize <addr> --block 54991182`, compared with the same artifacts. 7 of 7 equal.

vaultCoreCreationCode.claim: The vaults this deployment will produce are byte-identical to what b1cde122 builds, and that was read off the chain rather than inferred from VaultDeployer's own runtime.
vaultCoreCreationCode.how: VaultDeployer holds VaultCore's creation code in two SSTORE2 data contracts, not in its own 938 B runtime, so its runtime says nothing about what it will deploy. `codeChunkA()` returns 0x3B15efeCB5E6520471cD31E36204182f1708c0c1 (11,196 B) and `codeChunkB()` returns 0x55442569F98c82fF9CF06616aD0826fad6a9BD50 (11,197 B); `cast code` on both, each stripped of its leading SSTORE2 STOP byte and concatenated, gives 22,391 bytes that equal `out/VaultCore.sol/VaultCore.json` `bytecode.object` EXACTLY.
vaultCoreCreationCode.whyItMatters: A singleton codesize check on VaultDeployer is silent about the bytecode of every vault it will ever create. Reading the chunks is the only on-chain evidence for that, and it is the check this deployment's currency claim turned on while nothing had been stamped from them. THAT CLAUSE IS NOW OVERTAKEN: this key used to end 'no vault exists yet to measure instead', and two vaults do exist — `smokeVault.runtimeCodesize` and `secondVault.runtimeCodesize` below both record 20650, read with `cast codesize` at block 61,646,791. The chunk read is still the stronger evidence, because it is what the deployer will stamp from NEXT; a deployed vault's codesize is evidence about a vault already made. Both are recorded, and they agree.

oracle.note: C-6 launch model: ONE genuine Chainlink Data Feed per asset, no multi-source median and no quorum. `deployment.mjs` reads each asset's single `feed` as a one-element source set. The settlement token is pinned inside the oracle and is deliberately absent from `assets` — the constructor rejects a token that is both pinned and listed (ChainlinkOracle.sol:151). This oracle is the sole entry in the factory's oracle allowlist: `oracleAllowlistEnforced()` is true and `isAllowedOracle(0x79279FBa…)` is true, both read at block 54,991,182.
oracle.usdcNote: READ BACK from `ChainlinkOracle.usdc()`, and the token it names is USDG, not Circle USDC — `symbol()` returns "USDG", `decimals()` returns 6, both read at block 54,991,182. The key keeps the name `usdc` because that is the name the contract's own getter and `scripts/soak/deployment.mjs` use. `priceWad(0x5fc5360D…)` returns exactly 1e18, which is the pin, not a feed reading.
oracle.maxStalenessNote: A CHAIN READ ON THIS RECORD, unlike the Base Sepolia record's, which states plainly that its 86400 came from a config file because ChainlinkOracle exposes no `maxStalenessSeconds()` getter. It still does not — but staleness is a per-asset heartbeat and the heartbeat IS readable, as the second member of the public `feedOf` struct. `feedOf(WETH).heartbeat` and `feedOf(cbBTC).heartbeat` both return 86400 at block 54,991,182, so this number is what the two assets carry on chain and the value is theirs, not a configuration's. 86,400 s is `ChainlinkOracle.MAX_HEARTBEAT` exactly (ChainlinkOracle.sol:98) — the loosest bound the constructor accepts, so a price up to a day old is served without reverting. MAX_HEARTBEAT itself is a private constant and reverts when called; the ceiling is read from the source, not the chain.
oracle.sequencerUptimeFeedNote: address(0), read back from `ChainlinkOracle.sequencerUptimeFeed()` at block 54,991,182 — an owner-approved exemption of 2026-09-04, not an omission. Chainlink publishes no L2 Sequencer Uptime Feed for chain 4663, and the Base mainnet feed is not portable (0xBCF85224fc0756B9Fa45aA7892530B47e10b6433 has zero bytes of code here). WHAT THE CONTRACT DOES WITH IT: `_requireSequencerUp` opens with `if (address(seq) == address(0)) return;` (ChainlinkOracle.sol:314), so the guard is skipped and this oracle serves prices straight through a sequencer outage rather than reverting. It fails OPEN. `GRACE_PERIOD()` reads 3600 on chain but never applies while the feed is zero. What is left carrying a bad price is the per-asset heartbeat — at its ceiling here — and the sane-price band. The exemption that let the deploy script accept a zero feed on this chain is PR #203, merged 2026-09-05T05:11:24Z and therefore present in sourceCommit b1cde122; `contracts/config/robinhood-mainnet.json` still describes #203 as open and unmerged, which was true when that file was written and is stale now. The consequence is unchanged by the deploy: the sequencer guard has still never executed against a live feed, on this chain or any other.

execution.adapterNote: NO ADAPTER IS A PROTOCOL SINGLETON ON THIS CHAIN, and that is the mainnet design rather than an unfinished step. This key used to open 'NO ADAPTER IS DEPLOYED ON THIS CHAIN', which stopped being true once a vault was created with one: 0xc83B9CE8a12B8aca3f5f7d1C20383d60B1ECaA5E has 1,981 bytes of runtime on 4663 and is allow-listed by both vaults in this record. A per-vault adapter supplied by a creator is exactly what the design below describes; what does not exist is an adapter among the singletons. `contracts/script/Deploy.s.sol:33` states it directly — oracles and execution adapters are not protocol singletons, each vault creator supplies its own — and the only script in the repository that deploys an `AggregationRouterAdapter` is `DeployTestnet.s.sol`, which was not run here. The ten broadcast transactions contain no adapter. The field is null rather than absent so that a reader looking for it finds this note instead of an ambiguity, and the router address below is deliberately NOT written here: a router and an adapter are different contracts, and putting one under the other's key would be exactly the mislabeling `scripts/soak/deployment.mjs` was written to defend against. CONSEQUENCE FOR THE PARSER, stated so it is not discovered as a surprise: `parseDeployment` requires `execution.AggregationRouterAdapter` to be a 20-byte address, so it throws on this record — `deployment: AggregationRouterAdapter is not a 20-byte address: null` — and it is the ONLY field it throws on. The parser assumes the testnet-shaped deployment it was written against. Nothing here should be changed to make it pass, and neither should the parser: a soak run started against an adapterless record would fail later and less legibly.
execution.routerName: Uniswap SwapRouter02 (Robinhood Chain mainnet). Not at the canonical cross-chain SwapRouter02 address 0x68b3465833fb72A70ecDF485E0e4C7bD8665Fc45, which has zero bytes of code on 4663.

verifiedWiring.note: Every row read from chain 4663 with `cast call --block 54991182` against the addresses in `singletons`, EXCEPT `factory.vaultCount()` — see the next key. The four REVERSE-direction edges are listed first and deliberately: a forward read can agree with an address book that is itself wrong, and only the reverse edges catch that. verifiedWiring.vaultCountNote: `factory.vaultCount()` is the one row that is NOT a block-54,991,182 read, because it is the one row that changes. It read 0 at that block and reads 2 at block 61,513,974 (whose own timestamp 1789257623 is 2026-09-13T00:00:23Z — this parenthetical read 2026-09-12 until 2026-09-13, off by 23 seconds past midnight UTC, and every other date in this record is the block's own UTC timestamp). Every other row above is a wiring edge between immutable singletons and cannot move; this row is a counter, so pinning it to the deploy block would have frozen a number whose whole purpose is to go up. It is re-read, not re-derived: `cast call 0xc44B853F037b4fF33B831C9a2B341686dEC88Fd1 'vaultCount()(uint256)'`.

allowSubVaultsNote: `factory.allowSubVaults()` RETURNS FALSE — read from chain 4663 at block 54,991,182, and corroborated independently by the constructor arguments recovered from `cast tx 0x655991c7… input`, whose sixth word is zero. This is the launch parameter, and it is the observed state of a live deployment rather than an intention: sub-vaults are off, so this deployment is root-vaults-only, which is what closes C-1 (docs/LAUNCH-READINESS.md gate 0). It is the opposite of the Base Sepolia record's TRUE, and that asymmetry is deliberate there — that testnet keeps sub-vaults enabled because the SV-7 look-through soak drill needs a child vault to exercise. Do not read either value as drift from the other. The factory constructor takes this flag once and the factory is immutable, so it cannot be changed on this deployment.
ownershipNote: MEASUREMENT: `owner()` reverts on all six singletons and on the oracle, called at block 54,991,182 — these contracts expose no such getter. Recorded as an observation about what was read, and it is not by itself a description of what any party can or cannot do; the authority questions belong to the source and to docs/LAUNCH-READINESS.md, not to an address book.

intendedCreator.readback: Read at block 54,991,182: 171 bytes of code, `VERSION()` "1.4.1", `getThreshold()` 1, `getOwners()` [0x0f80606a2283fD9C67cE2eEC79B90E95907F9f35]. A threshold-1 single-owner Safe is a 1-of-1 — an address with a different failure surface from the EOA behind it, not a multisig, and it does not by itself satisfy an operational gate asking for shared custody.
intendedCreator.why: `VaultFactory.createVault` is permissionless and `msg.sender` becomes both the vault's creator and its attested operator (VaultFactory.sol:183-184, attestation at :195); `VaultCore.creator` is immutable (VaultCore.sol:73); and `VaultParams` carries no field for either identity (VaultFactory.sol:172-181). So the creating account is fixed at creation and cannot be corrected afterwards. The Base Sepolia smoke vault was created by the deployer EOA and that record states the consequence: the first vault here must be created BY THE SAFE, not by a script from the EOA.

smokeVault.stateCorroboration: `state` HOLDS 21 ROWS: 19 read off the vault and 2 off the factory. ALL 19 VAULT-LEVEL ROWS WERE RE-READ AT HEAD ON 2026-09-13, block 62,119,813, and all 19 are identical. COUNT THEM RATHER THAN TAKING THE NUMBER: an earlier version of this note said 22 and 20, carried from the issue that asked for the port instead of counted from the object, and PR #253's block has the same 21 keys, so the issue was wrong rather than the port. 2,909,847 blocks separate the two reads, so the agreement is not a coincidence of timing. TWELVE OF THE 19 CANNOT MOVE, and the split is taken from the declarations rather than from this sentence: ten are `immutable` in `VaultCore` (`creator`, `usdc`, `oracle`, `governance`, `feeEngine`, `operatorRegistry`, `capacityCapUsdc`, `minDepositUsdc`, `exitFeeMaxBps`, `exitFeeDecayPeriod`); `basketLength()` is the length of `basketAssets`, assigned once in the constructor with no setter and no push site; and `parentVault()` is not an immutable at all but a derived read that returns `address(0)` whenever `subVaultRegistry` is zero, which is permanent here because the factory was constructed with `allowSubVaults` false. THE SEVEN THAT CAN MOVE — `totalShares`, `navWad`, `idleUsdc`, `holderCount`, `nonCreatorMemberCount`, `sharesOf(creator)`, `totalQueuedShares` — have not, because nothing has deposited into or exited this vault since. THE TWO FACTORY ROWS ARE THE EXCEPTION AND ARE DELIBERATELY LEFT AS READ: `factory.vaultCount()` was 1 at block 59,209,966 and is 2 today, and rewriting it would destroy the one-consistent-state property this block rests on. `factory.allVaults(0)` still returns this vault. A reader who wants the count as of now reads `verifiedWiring` and `secondVault`, not this object.

explorerVerificationNote: ALL SEVEN CONTRACTS ARE SOURCE-VERIFIED, on Sourcify and on the Blockscout explorer, and both were read back for this note rather than carried over. SOURCIFY: `GET https://sourcify.dev/server/v2/contract/4663/<address>` returns `creationMatch` exact_match AND `runtimeMatch` exact_match for every one of the seven. The creation check and the runtime check are separate matches and both are exact, which is the strongest answer that endpoint gives. EXPLORER: `GET https://robinhoodchain.blockscout.com/api/v2/smart-contracts/<address>` returns `is_verified` true and `is_partially_verified` false for every one of the seven. Both sweeps were run again on 2026-09-05, contract by contract, with a browser User-Agent. AGAINST WHICH SOURCE: the tree at `sourceCommit` b1cde122, the same commit `bytecodeCurrency` above pins, compiled with solc 0.8.26+commit.8a97fa7a, which is the `compiler_version` the explorer reports for all seven. THE LICENCE HEADER ON THE VERIFIED SOURCE IS BUSL-1.1, in all 27 source files across the seven contracts, read out of Sourcify's own `sources` payload. That is the header the code was compiled and broadcast with. The repository relicensed from BUSL-1.1 to MIT afterwards, on 2026-09-05, in PR #223, so the repository today and the verified source deliberately disagree: an explorer shows the source a deployment was built from, and that source cannot change after the fact. Do not "fix" the explorer to match the repository. The explorer's own `license_type` field reads "none" for all seven, which is a field nobody set rather than a licence claim. A WARNING FOR WHOEVER READS THIS BACK: the explorer's `/api/v2/smart-contracts/` endpoint answers HTTP 500 intermittently on contracts that are verified. VaultDeployer needed several attempts, and while it was still failing, `/api/v2/search?q=<address>` reported `is_smart_contract_verified` true and `/api/v2/addresses/<address>` reported `is_verified` true for the same address. A 500 from that endpoint is a server error, NOT an answer that a contract is unverified; retry it or read one of the other two. This note supersedes the earlier state in which an automated client was refused with HTTP 403 behind a bot challenge and `forge verify-contract` failed at the ABI lookup before submitting; that challenge was never worked around. How verification was ultimately accepted is not something these read-backs establish, and nothing here should be read as asserting a mechanism. WHAT HAS NOT CHANGED: source verification is an explorer convenience and is still not what establishes the identity of these contracts. `bytecodeCurrency` above is, by byte-for-byte comparison against the b1cde122 artifacts, and it depends on no explorer. What verification adds is that a reader who does not build the tree can read the source beside the bytecode. docs/DEPLOYMENT.md carries the same three facts and the two endpoint URLs.
